paras: The lynching of Reuben Elrod was the shooting death of an elderly Black man by a band of white men at his home near Piedmont, Anderson County, South Carolina, on the night of June 30, 1903. The men also beat the Black women who lived in the house and ordered them to leave, and an inquest found that Elrod had died at the hands of parties unknown. South Carolina papers reported that the killing was condemned around Piedmont, and the Black press later counted it among the lynchings of 1903.

Elrod was described in every dispatch as a respected old man; the Keowee Courier put his age at about 70 and said he had never been in trouble with white people. The New-York Tribune called the women who shared his house "his relatives," while the Anderson Intelligencer's local correspondent wrote that Elrod had the reputation of keeping "loose negro women" about his place.

About 10 o'clock that Tuesday night, a group of white men came to Elrod's cabin on a lonely road outside Piedmont. According to the women's testimony at the inquest, about fifty men shot and killed Elrod, then beat the women and warned them to leave. The Intelligencer's correspondent gave a different sequence: the men demanded the women, and in the wrangle a single shot fired at random through the weatherboarding struck Elrod in the throat. In that account his body fell on a lighted lamp and was burned, and two women said they were beaten with sticks and ordered to leave.

Magistrate Bowen held an inquest on July 1, and the jury found that Elrod came to his death at the hands of parties unknown. The women said they did not recognize their attackers; the local correspondent wrote that they were "evidently cowed" and would not swear to anyone's identity. A Columbia dispatch reported that no one had been apprehended, and no report of an arrest, indictment or trial appears in the later coverage.

The fullest early report was an Anderson special of July 1 to The State and the Greenville News, reprinted by South Carolina weeklies under headlines from "Old Negro Slain; Women Whipped" to "Lynching Near Piedmont" and "Whitecaps in Anderson." A shorter Columbia wire ran on July 2 in the New-York Tribune as "Negro Killed Defending Women" and in the Savannah Morning News as "They Killed a Negro and Whipped Women," and a one-line digest reached Midwestern weeklies.

These reports called the attack the work of a mob and said the community deplored it, yet they also passed on the "general supposition" that the women were "objectionable" and that "a posse of citizens" had gone to chastise them, with Elrod killed when he resisted. Local commentary divided: the Abbeville Press and Banner, under "Race Troubles," wrote that the women were beaten for offending "the murderous mob's idea of good morals." The Anderson Intelligencer headed its account "Murder at Piedmont" but presented the shot as meant to scare and called it "a case of men becoming lawless for the sake of punishing law-breakers."

In the Black press, the Savannah Tribune printed the Columbia dispatch on its front page on July 4 as "Gory Work of Whitecaps," saying Elrod was shot "for some unknown reason" and omitting the community's explanation about the women. Six months later the Chicago Broad Ax's chronology of 1903 listed Elrod under lynchings for July 1, beside Charles Evans of Norway, South Carolina.

The women's sworn testimony put the attackers at about fifty, while the Intelligencer's correspondent judged they "must have been few in numbers" and reported town opinion that the fatal shot was meant only to scare. The wire and State reports counted three women in the house; the Intelligencer counted two.

reader.title: Lynching of Reuben Elrod
bases: A band of white men came to Elrod's house at night to whip and drive out the women living there, killed Elrod by gunfire, and beat the women and ordered them away (A4, A9, A25).

Elrod was shot dead in his home by a group of white men (about fifty by the women's sworn testimony, a 'company of men' by the local correspondent) with no lawful authority, who came to punish and expel women judged 'objectionable' or 'loose' (A4, A9); papers called it a lynching and the Broad Ax listed it among the year's lynchings (A7, A26).

The State's Anderson special, the Columbia wire, an independent Greenville Mountaineer correspondent and the Keowee Courier agree that a group of white men shot Elrod in his home at night, beat the women and ordered them away, and that the inquest found parties unknown, though they differ on details (A2, A4, A9, A25).

The Columbia wire ran in New York and Savannah under 'Negro Killed Defending Women' and 'They Killed a Negro and Whipped Women', and as a one-line digest item in Midwestern weeklies.

The Anderson Intelligencer headed it 'Murder at Piedmont' and reported universal condemnation, but described the women as 'loose', the shot as meant to scare, and the attackers as men 'punishing law-breakers'.
The Abbeville Press and Banner, under 'Race Troubles', said the women were beaten for offending 'the murderous mob's idea of good morals'.
The Savannah Tribune headed the dispatch 'Gory Work of Whitecaps', added that Elrod was shot 'for some unknown reason', and dropped the community's explanation about the women.
The Chicago Broad Ax counted Elrod among the lynchings of 1903 in its year-end chronology.
